transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Embercrest Head of Cloud Partnerships), Tomás Rivera (Embercrest Infrastructure Lead), Sarah Ng (Embercrest Solutions Architect)

Summary:
Light partner discovery focused on integrating Embercrest's managed GPU clusters as an onramp for Redwood Dedicated/private customers. Main themes: network topology options (VPC peering vs private control plane), KMS/encryption and audit log requirements, perf expectations across GPU shapes, model compatibility/quantization discussions, and pilot scope/next steps.

Topics:
- Onramp architecture choices (managed gateway, private control plane)
- Security and compliance (KMS/HSM, SOC 2, audit logs, data residency)
- Performance profiles and sample workloads (batching, KV cache, seq len)
- Commercial/pilot framing and responsibilities

Action items (as captured in call): Jordan to run perf matrix; Maya to share docs/terms; Sarah to provide dataset/QPS profiles.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): All right hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round-robin? We got, uh, Lena, Tomás and Sarah from Embercrest, and Jordan's with me from SE. Can you hear okay?
[00:12] Lena (Embercrest): Yep loud and clear. Thanks, Maya. Appreciate you squeezing this in.
[00:18] Jordan (Redwood SE): Great. I'll kick off with a 10-minute sketch of how we typically wire partners like Embercrest into Redwood Dedicated and private deployments, then we can jump into specifics.
[00:26] Tomás (Embercrest): Sounds good. We're interested in technical constraints first, then commercial later. We're trying not to, you know, bake assumptions about network or storage.
[00:35] Maya: Perfect. High level: two common integration patterns — lightweight onramp where you expose a managed gateway that routes requests to Embercrest GPU pools, or full private control plane where we install a small control-plane agent in your VPC and route control traffic over mTLS.
[00:48] Sarah: When you say "managed gateway" — is that internet-facing? We have strict egress rules.
[00:54] Jordan: Good question. Managed gateway can be put behind a static IP + allowlist and support TLS. But for stricter setups we do the private control-plane option so no public endpoints for inferencing traffic — it's routed over private links/peered networks.
[01:06] Tomás: We prefer peered/private. We also need to understand KMS. Embercrest runs HashiCorp Vault backed with HSM in our colo. Does Redwood integrate with external KMS or only cloud KMS options?
[01:17] Maya: We support both. For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS via PKCS#11 or Vault; there's a compatibility matrix. We'll send the KMS integration notes after the call.
[01:26] Lena: Great. We also need audit logs and per-customer tenancy. Our compliance folks will want to see how tokens and payloads are retained.
[01:33] Jordan: On audit logs — Redwood logs request/response metadata and can optionally include hashes of payloads. We support configurable retention for audit events and can route logs into your SIEM via syslog or S3 with encryption at rest.
[01:45] Sarah: What's the latency profile if we run models locally on Embercrest infra versus routing to Redwood-hosted fallback? We have some real-time features where 200-300ms matters.
[01:54] Jordan: For local execution on medium NVIDIA "A40-ish" shapes we typically see mid-100ms token latencies for small context windows when batching is minimized. But that varies with model size and sequence length. If we fallback to a smaller quantized variant in another region, that might add 20-80ms depending on routing.
[02:10] Tomás: You said "A40-ish" — our fleet includes a mix: A10s and some newer Hopper cards. We need to understand memory/kv cache implications.
[02:18] Jordan: Hopper helps with larger KV cache and lower per-token CPU overhead. For KV caching you'll want a dedicated instance w/ larger host memory. We also recommend using Redwood's automatic prefix caching to reduce repeated tokens; that'll reduce egress and cost.
[02:30] Lena: On cost — we're trying to pitch this as an add-on to customers. Do you have a simple unit econ model? Cost per token on Dedicated vs hosted?
[02:38] Maya: We provide sample cost curves. For Dedicated we do a blended price by GPU-shape + utilization and concurrency. We'll draft a sample with Embercrest profile. Jordan can run perf numbers to feed that.
[02:47] Sarah: Any gotchas on model compatibility? We have customers running Llama variants and some custom fine-tuned models. Does Redwood need specific conversions or compilation steps?
[02:56] Jordan: We support common model formats (HF PT, GGML-ish exports, ONNX for some cases) and do automatic kernel selection. For some custom ops we may need a build step. For quantized paths we have guidance. There will be edge cases with custom FLAIR ops — occasionally we need to ship a tiny shim.
[03:11] Tomás: Ok. For pilot scope, we were thinking: a 2-week ramp where Embercrest exposes a medium GPU cluster, Redwood runs a handful of customer workloads (3 models), and we measure latency/cost and verify audit/KMS. Is that in line?
[03:21] Maya: Yeah that sounds right. Typical pilot roles: Embercrest provides infra + network access and support; Redwood provides runtime, instrumented tests, and a small dev account. We usually ask for a non-production test dataset and a sample QPS profile.
[03:31] Lena: We can do that. Sarah will share dataset characteristics after this.
[03:35] Sarah: Yep I'll drop it in the shared folder. One question — how do you handle multi-tenant isolation? We need strong boundaries between customers on the same GPU node.
[03:44] Jordan: Isolation is logical at the runtime level — namespaces, per-tenant KV caches, and optional container isolation if you want physical separation. We can run per-tenant dedicated pools for higher assurance.
[03:52] Tomás: How about autoscaling? We want to avoid noisy neighbor spikes.
[03:57] Jordan: Redwood supports autoscaler with policy controls — per-customer min/max, burst windows, and circuit breakers. For partner onramps we typically recommend a headroom policy to protect baseline latency.
[04:06] Maya: Quick note on routing: we can do latency-first routing (use nearest Embercrest pool), cost-first (use quantized variant or preemptible hardware), or hybrid. Sounds like Embercrest will pick latency-first for real-time features.
[04:18] Lena: Correct. Another compliance item — data residency. Some of our customers require tokens to never leave EMEA. Does Redwood respect region pinning?
[04:26] Maya: Yes. We can pin model execution to specified regions or on-prem. For private deployments, all inference can stay within your region and we can disable global fallback. There are tradeoffs (capacity, cost).
[04:36] Sarah: Could you talk about monitoring and traces? Our ops team will want per-request traces and model output diffs for audits.
[04:41] Jordan: Redwood Console has per-route traces, token-level latency breakdowns, and a diffs feature for model regressions tied to prompt sets. We can export traces to your tracing backend as well. Some customers use that to drive rollback automation.
[04:55] Tomás: Are there any special network ports or protocols we should plan for? We're trying to schedule a firewall change window.
[05:01] Jordan: For private control-plane we use mTLS over 443 by default; for managed gateway it's standard HTTPS. If using gRPC we recommend allowing 443/80 outbound. We'll share a minimal ports list.
[05:12] Maya: I also want to flag one common ops concern — model weight syncing. If you're hosting, we can pull model weights via secure pull from Embercrest blobstore or you can push an image. Both are supported; syncing large weights over slower links may require rsync or pre-seeding.
[05:26] Sarah: We can pre-seed in colo.
[05:28] Lena: On the commercial side: what does a partner revenue share look like for a channel arrangement? We're exploring reseller and co-sell.
[05:35] Maya: There are a few patterns — reseller markup on top of Dedicated seats, referral fees, or co-sell where Embercrest bundles Redwood as part of a managed offering and we provide partner discounts. I'll share a short partner framework doc.
[05:45] Tomás: Any legal issues in the pilot MSA? Our procurement usually pushes for limited liability and clear termination.
[05:51] Maya: We'll share a sample MSA and pilot addendum. For pilots we do a short addendum with scope, SLAs for the pilot, and an acceptance criteria.
[05:59] Jordan: Quick deep-dive note — quantization: for 4-bit/8-bit paths some operators may produce slight output distribution shifts. We'll include recommended eval prompts to validate quality margins so you can measure if a quantized fallback is acceptable.
[06:14] Sarah: Perfect. Could you also include sample eval harness and suggested prompt sets?
[06:19] Jordan: Yes. We'll attach an example eval kit and a spreadsheet for results.
[06:24] Lena: I think that's most of it. Any blockers from Redwood?
[06:28] Maya: Nothing immediate. We'll need access to a test cluster and firewall rules, and we'll start with a small set of SSO users for the pilot.
[06:36] Tomás: We can stand that up. We'll carve out a CIDR and idp group.
[06:40] Maya: Wrap-up then. Next steps: Jordan runs perf matrix, Maya shares security/KMS/MSA docs, Sarah provides dataset and QPS. We'll aim to have pilot kickoff week of April 20th if timelines hold.
[06:52] Lena: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[06:55] Maya: Thanks all — I'll send notes and links.
